911.quote_or_event: “Meekly and politely they approach him with their manifold arts to win his heart; and talking sweetly in confidential conversation they make him do (what they like).”
911.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that sweet, intimate talk is the tool by which a man is led wherever the woman wants.
911.tie_back: Kural 911 also warns that the sweet words of women who want a man's money, not the man, end in disgrace and grief.
911._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The danger of sweet words matches, but the Jain verse does not mention the money motive that defines Kural 911.

912.quote_or_event: “A young woman, putting on fine ornaments and clothes, will say to a Sramana: 'I shall give up (my former way of life) and practise the rough (viz. control). Reverend sir, teach me the Law!'”
912.explanation: The text describes a woman who talks piously of religion in order to win over a monk, and it warns him not to trust that show of virtue.
912.tie_back: This fits Kural 912's women who first weigh their profit and then 'speak of virtue' (panburaikkum), so that the wise man must weigh their character and stay away.
912._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Jacobi's diacritic Śramaṇa simplified to Sramana). The pretended virtue is a close match, but the woman's motive here is seduction, not profit.

913.quote_or_event: Jain monks and devout lay people meditate on twelve reflections (anupreksha). The sixth is asuchi, the impurity of the body, which Sangave renders as the body being impure and dirty.
913.explanation: Jainism weakens physical desire by meditating on the body as perishable and impure, not as a source of real joy.
913.tie_back: Kural 913 likens the false embrace of a woman who wants only money to clasping a stranger's corpse in a dark room, a shock image of the same kind as the Jain reflection on the body's impurity.
913.source: Asuchi anupreksha, as described in V.A. Sangave, 'Jaina ethics' (jainworld.com); cf. Tattvartha Sutra ch. 9 on the twelve reflections
913._accuracy_note: Wording checked on Sangave's page. It only shares the device of a repellent bodily image, because the Kural's simile is about the falseness of the embrace while asuchi is about the body itself. Next-best match.

914.quote_or_event: Jain tradition remembers the monk Sthulabhadra, who had once loved the courtesan Kosha. As a monk he asked to spend the rainy season in her house, and at its end his teacher Sambhutavijaya praised him above two disciples who had spent it in a lion's cave and on a wheel.
914.explanation: The story is told to show that a man devoted to the spiritual path can stand amid a courtesan's charms without being moved by them.
914.tie_back: It illustrates Kural 914: the wise, who seek the wealth of grace (arut-porul), will not touch the cheap charms (punnalam) of women for whom money is everything.
914.source: Hemachandra, Parisistaparvan VIII.109-169, as summarised from Jinaprabhasuri's Vividhatirthakalpa (OpenEdition / wisdomlib.org)
914._accuracy_note: The summary was verified on wisdomlib; the full Parisistaparvan text was not read. The story is about a monk's self-mastery rather than a householder avoiding courtesans, and Kosha is not portrayed only as mercenary.

915.quote_or_event: “...cohabitation with a harlot–itvarikā aparigṛhītāgamana... are the five transgressions of the fourth minor vow of contentment with one’s wife (svadārasantoṣa aṇuvrata).”
915.explanation: Umasvati's Tattvartha Sutra makes going to a prostitute a formal breach of the Jain householder's vow of sexual restraint.
915.tie_back: Kural 915 says those of mature understanding will not seek the 'common' charms (podhu-nalam) of paid women, and Jain lay ethics makes this a vow.
915.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.28 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018, wisdomlib.org)
915._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; ellipses mark omitted items in the list. A precise doctrinal match on avoiding prostitutes, though a legal rule, not a reflection on wisdom.

916.quote_or_event: “In the assembly he pronounces holy (words), yet secretly he commits sins; but the wise know him to be a deceiver and great rogue.”
916.explanation: The Sutrakritanga says that a man who hides his sexual lapses still loses his good name among the discerning.
916.tie_back: Kural 916 says that those who care about their own good name stay away from women who sell their favours, and this verse shows how such a lapse destroys that reputation.
916._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The verse is about a hypocritical monk; the link through lost reputation is real but indirect.

917.quote_or_event: “One man (women) have in their heart, another in their words, and another still in their actions. Therefore a monk should not trust women, knowing that they are full of deceit.”
917.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that the one whose embrace a man receives may have her heart set on someone else.
917.tie_back: This mirrors Kural 917's women who embrace while 'cherishing another in their hearts' (pira-nenjil peni), and the steady, self-governed heart (nirai-nenjam) needed to resist them.
917._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The divided heart is a near one-to-one match. The Jain verse generalises about all women, while the Kural speaks only of mercenary ones.

918.quote_or_event: “As (men by baiting) with a piece of flesh a fearless single lion get him into a trap, so women may capture an ascetic though he be careful.”
918.explanation: The Sutrakritanga presents seduction as a snare that catches even the strong and wary.
918.tie_back: Kural 918 compares the embrace of deceitful women to seizure by an enchanting spirit (anangu) that ruins those who do not look closely, the same image of a man captured.
918._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. The trap image matches, but the Kural's supernatural anangu has no counterpart here, and Jainism does not attribute the fall to an outside spirit.

919.quote_or_event: “As an elephant, sinking down in a quagmire, sees the raised ground but does not get to the shore, so do we who long for sensual pleasures, not follow the path of monks.”
919.explanation: King Brahmadatta admits to the sage Citra that he is stuck in sensual pleasure like an elephant in mud, and the lecture ends with him sinking into the deepest hell.
919.tie_back: It closely matches Kural 919's picture of the soft arms of women without limits as a hell-like mire into which undiscerning men sink.
919.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.30, cf. 13.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
919._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The mire and hell imagery are strikingly close, though Brahmadatta's pleasures are general sensual ones, not specifically courtesans.

920.quote_or_event: Jain codes of lay conduct (shravakachara texts) list seven vices (vyasanas) that a layman must give up completely: gambling, drinking alcohol, eating meat, sexual promiscuity (visiting prostitutes), hunting, theft and adultery.
920.explanation: The seven-vice list ties prostitution, drink and gambling together as addictions that ruin a householder.
920.tie_back: Kural 920 groups exactly these, double-minded women, liquor and dice, as the companions of those whom fortune has abandoned.
920.source: Saptavyasana (seven vices) of the Jain shravakachara literature; glossary entry 'Vyasana', JAINpedia (Institute of Jainology)
920._accuracy_note: The list was checked on JAINpedia's glossary and paraphrased. It contains all three of the Kural's vices; no primary shravakachara verse was read in this session.
